{{Short description|Mathematical constant; sum of 1 / 2^2^n}}
{{for|the smallest positive integer m such that n divides m!|Kempner function}}
{{infobox non-integer number
|title=Kempner number
|rationality=Transcendental
|decimal=0.81642150902189314370... {{OEIS|A007404}}
|binary=0.11010001000000010000... {{OEIS|A036987}}
|continued_fraction_linear=[0;1,4,2,4,4,6,4,2,4,6,...] {{OEIS|A007400}}

The '''Kempner number'''<ref name=adamczewski>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Adamczewski |first1=Boris |title=The many faces of the Kempner number |date=2013 |class=math.NT |eprint=1303.1685}}; also published as [https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/vol16.html ''Journal of Integer Sequences'' '''16''' (2013), article 13.2.15.]</ref> is the sum of the series 
:::<math>\kappa:=2^{-2^0} + 2^{-2^1} + 2^{-2^2} + \cdots = \sum_{n\ge 0} 2^{-2^n}.</math>  
It is named after [[Aubrey Kempner]], who proved it [[transcendental number|transcendental]] in 1916.<ref name=kempner>On Transcendental Numbers, A. J. Kempner, ''Transactions of the American Mathematical Society'', '''17''', #4 (1916), pp. 476-482, {{mr|1501054}}, {{doi|10.1090/s0002-9947-1916-1501054-4}}.</ref>  It is an example of a number easy to prove transcendental which is not a [[Liouville number]].<ref name=adamczewski />{{rp|at=§1}}
==Properties==
By definition, the binary expansion of the Kempner number has zeroes everywhere except at places which are powers of two:
:κ = 0.110100010000000100000000000000010000000000000000000000000000000100...     (base two.)
Since the first proof of transcendence by Kempner, many other proofs have been given; see the references.<ref name=adamczewski /><ref>Section 13.3, ''Automatic Sequences: Theory, Applications, Generalizations'', Jean-Paul Allouche, Jeffrey Shallit, Cambridge University Press, 2003, ISBN 9780521823326, {{doi|10.1017/CBO9780511546563}}.</ref><ref>Note on a theorem of Kempner concerning transcendental numbers, H. Blumberg, ''Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society'' '''32''' (1926), pp. 351–356, {{doi|10.1090/s0002-9904-1926-04222-1}}.</ref><ref>Arithmetische Eigenschaften der Lösungen einer Klasse von Funktionalgleichungen, K. Mahler, ''Mathematische Annalen'' '''101''' (1929), pp. 342–366, {{doi|10.1007/BF01454845}}. Corrigendum, '''103''' (1930), p. 532, {{doi|10.1007/BF01455708}}.</ref><ref>Algebraic independence properties of the Fredholm series, J. H. Loxton and A. J. van der Poorten, ''Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society, Series A'', '''26''', #1 (1978), pp. 31–45, {{doi|10.1017/S1446788700011472 }}.</ref><ref>An "Oceans of zeros" proof that a certain non-Liouville number is transcendental, M. J. Knight, ''The American Mathematical Monthly'', '''98''', #10 (December 1991), pp. 947–949, {{doi|10.2307/2324154}}, {{JSTOR|2324154}}.</ref><ref>Theorem 1.1.2, ''Mahler Functions and Transcendence'', Kumiko Nishioka, Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer-Verlag, 1996, ISBN 3-540-61472-9, {{doi|10.1007/BFb0093672}}. Volume 1631 of ''[[Lecture Notes in Mathematics]]''. </ref><ref>[https://people.math.sc.edu/filaseta/gradcourses/Math785/Math785Notes5.pdf "The Beginnings of Transcendental Numbers"], Michael Filaseta, lecture notes, Math 785, Transcendental Number Theory, Spring 2011, University of South Carolina. Accessed Jan. 22, 2026.</ref>

[[Jeffrey Shallit]] has proven that it has a simple [[continued fraction]] expansion, obtainable by the following construction:<ref name="shallit1979">Simple continued fractions for some irrational numbers, Jeffrey Shallit, ''Journal of Number Theory'', '''11''', #2 (May 1979), pp. 209-217, {{doi|10.1016/0022-314X(79)90040-4}}.</ref>{{rp|at=Theorem 1}}
# Start with the partial expansion {{math|1=[0, 1, 3]}}.
# If the partial expansion is {{math|1=[''a'', ''b'', ..., ''y'', ''z'']}}, replace it by {{math|1=[''a'', ''b'', ..., ''y'', ''z'' + ''1'', ''z'' &minus; 1, ''y'', ..., ''b'']}}.
# If this generated a zero, replace {{math|1=[..., ''a'', 0, ''b'', ...]}} by {{math|1=[..., ''a'' + ''b'', ...]}}.
# Repeat steps 2 and 3 indefinitely.
This generates the expansion {{OEIS|A007400}}
:<math>[0; 1, 4, 2, 4, 4, 6, 4, 2, 4, 6, ...]=0+\cfrac {1}{1+\cfrac {1}{4+\cfrac {1}{2 + \cfrac{1}{4 + \ _{\ddots}}}}}.</math>
After the first partial quotients, the remainders are all 2, 4 or 6.  Since this continued fraction has bounded partial quotients, the Kempner number has [[irrationality measure]] 2.
